JPM.name: JPMorgan Chase
JPM.numbers_line: EPS $5.75 vs $5.93 est (miss; the call's own figure is $5.57 after $658M of securities losses in Corporate); revenue $50.2B vs $51.2B est; revenue +8% y/y, ROTCE 20%, net income $15.3B.
JPM.guidance: Q4 NII ex-markets ~$25.5B, total NII ~$28B; first 2027 central case for NII ex-markets ~$107B (about a quarter of the $5B uplift from the hikes in the curve, the rest balance-sheet growth); Q4 expense ~$27.5B, 2027 consensus of ~$114B 'not too far off'; card charge-off rate ~3.2%. Buyback cut to $1B from a ~$7B cadence because, in Dimon's words, they can now redeploy capital at better returns than buying stock at a 6% earnings yield.
call_said: Dimon is tightening credit: 'some of the credit terms have got a little bit loose' (too much vehicle, weak covenants, priming of good assets). The wholesale reserve build was new volume, not downgrades. He puts a higher chance than most on a market or economic stress event and says a 6% ten-year is not off the table.

AI agents and the deposit scare trade: Barnum calls it the intersection of two old things, yield-seeking flows and fintech competition; JPM is blocking outside agents from accounts (no credential sharing) while building its own. AI spend is ~$700M a year, benefits are 'not observable' in quarterly earnings yet, token cost is 'a whole other conversation'.

The quarter's shape: equities +49% (prime, derivatives), FICC -4%, IB fees +14% but activity 'slowed a bit' in the second half of September as rates sold off. Debit and credit spend +10%, 650k net new checking accounts, deposits +4%. Dimon expects the fourth quarter will not show the usual seasonal decline in markets: 'too much going on in the world'. AI-capex exposure is 'modest' but nobody would be immune to a sentiment change.
JPM.quote: "We are tightening up a little bit credit. I think some of the credit terms have got a little bit loose." — Jamie Dimon
JPM.read_through: Credit is still clean at the biggest lender but the terms are being pulled in and the buyback was parked; rising rates are an NII tailwind for every bank in the universe (BAC, WFC, C, USB, PNC), and the equity-financing boom is what carries GS and MS.

C.name: Citigroup
C.numbers_line: EPS $2.85 vs $2.66 est (beat); revenue $23.8B vs $23.7B est, the best third quarter in a decade; revenue +8%, net income +17%, ROTCE 11.5%.
C.guidance: Full-year ROTCE raised to 'above 11%' (was 10–11%); NII ex-markets growth to mid-to-high 6% (was 5–6%); efficiency ratio below 60%; card losses ~4%, the low end. Q4 markets seasonally down ~20% 'or possibly a bit more'. Banamex deconsolidation next year with an ~$9B CTA loss through the P&L in early 2027, slightly accretive to CET1. CET1 glide path to 13.1% by January 2028 under current rules. About $500M of the $5B investment plan pulled into the second half (half landed in Q3, ~$200M of it severance).
call_said: Fraser on the macro: conditions 'did soften a bit' in Q3. The corporate behavior change is tenor and format: syndicated debt and loan issuance moderated in favour of loans and revolvers as rates rose, and a three-year maturity wall is coming in a different rate and liquidity environment.

AI is a cost line that is already paying: 14,000 engineers on the Devin agentic coding tool, tech vendor spend down 30% y/y, ~100 manual processes being re-engineered; the financial benefit this year exceeds the investment. On the ecosystem: 'we are not seeing a slowdown in investment', compute and energy are the bottleneck, higher rates will not trump the imperative to invest.

Where the growth is: services +15% (ROTCE 31%), wealth +15% with $38B net new investment assets (+100%), equities +14% with prime balances +40%. Citi led the SK hynix equity raise (largest ever by an Asian issuer) and the $11B SoftBank high-yield deal (largest ever). Q&A pressure: the implied Q4 ROTCE in the high single digits looks 'really lousy' (Mayo); the CFO called it an abundance of caution.
C.quote: "We are not seeing a slowdown in investment in the broader AI ecosystem… Energy remains a bottleneck requiring more investment." — Jane Fraser
C.read_through: The AI build-out is still being financed through the banks' windows (SK hynix, SoftBank, Intel this quarter): good for the memory and chip pack's access to capital, and a bigger pile of AI-linked paper on bank balance sheets to watch.

GS.name: Goldman Sachs
GS.numbers_line: EPS $17.01 vs $12.86 est (large beat; ~$18 before a $450M accelerated charitable gift); revenue $18.7B vs $16.8B est, the second-highest quarter in the firm's history; ROE 18.7%, ROTE 20.5%.
GS.guidance: Alternatives fundraising now ~$150B for the year (started the year at $75–100B); incentive fees stay elevated in Q4; another 'meaningful' charitable contribution in Q4 (five years of giving pulled forward); tax rate ~20%; 30% comp ratio is the best estimate for the year; CET1 12.4% is a 100bp buffer; the big SLR balance-sheet extension is 'behind us'.
call_said: Equities $6.4B, +72%, equities financing +96% to a record on prime balances and Asia; demand for equity financing exceeds industry capacity so pricing is attractive. Financing is now over 40% of FICC plus equities revenue, the 'durable' base Solomon keeps pointing to.

AI capex: recent studies put the US data-center build at over $10 trillion through 2032 (~3.6% of GDP a year); demand for compute 'significantly exceeds supply'. Asked whether financing is the choke point, Solomon: 'I don't know and nobody knows', there will be a recalibration 'for sure', and hyperscaler-backed projects price very differently from the neo-clouds.

The environment went from 'top decile' in May and June to 'top quartile' now: a handful of IPOs pulled in September when valuations came in 10–15% light, sponsors still slow to monetise 2020–21 vintages, provisions $368M on idiosyncratic impairments. Advisory a record, lead over the next firm ~$430B. Solomon twice denied any succession timeline.
GS.quote: "As a 64-year-old guy… a 5% 10-year treasury doesn't scare me in terms of an operating environment." — David Solomon
GS.read_through: The capital for the AI cycle is still arriving (Hugging Face to NVIDIA at $13B this quarter); the risk GS names is cost of financing and crowding out, which lands first on the neo-clouds and data-centre borrowers in our universe (CRWV, NBIS, APLD, IREN), not the hyperscalers.

WFC.name: Wells Fargo
WFC.numbers_line: EPS $1.87 vs $1.85 est (small beat, +13% y/y); revenue $21.9B vs $22.3B est (light); revenue +2%, ROTCE 16.3%.
WFC.guidance: Full-year NII still ~$50B; Q4 NII ~$13B with NIM flat; 2026 expense ~$55.7B held despite ~$400M more revenue-related cost; CET1 managed 10–10.5% (now 10%); Basel III endgame could cut RWA ~7%; loan growth will beat the mid-single-digit guide. 2027: the Q4 exit rate is a better jump-off, more in January.
call_said: The markets miss was late September: the CFO had guided mid-single-digit markets growth at a conference, it came in flat as sharp rate moves hit fixed-income valuations and cut strategic, hedging and primary-issuance activity while equity volatility stayed low.

The consumer, in numbers: debit spend +8% (from 5% a year ago), credit spend +12%, charge-offs down, early-stage delinquencies at historic lows, fuel 3–6% of spend. 'We do not see signs of this yet, but we know that cycles are inevitable.' Auto is edging toward near-prime (5% of originations). CRE: higher rates mean lower valuations, 'it's just math', too early to see stress.

Scharf on AI agents moving deposits: 'completely overdone'. Tokenised deposits launched on its own chain (cross-border in under two minutes); a 21-bank consortium stablecoin in H1 2027; headcount down 30% from the 2020 peak; 'very hard limits' on AI-infrastructure lending.
WFC.quote: "The idea that that's going to contribute to mass movement to higher rate alternatives, I think, is completely overdone." — Charlie Scharf
WFC.read_through: Consumer spending and credit are intact at the most consumer-heavy big bank; the same September rates shock that hit WFC's trading desk is the one that cooled IB at JPM and pulled IPOs at GS. Watch WFC's card vintages and near-prime auto as the first place a consumer turn would show.
